The electromagnetic field considered has the form A_ext = x^+ (x^-) dx^-, with the only non-zero component of the field strength being F_-+ = E(x^-).
There is a classical 'electromagnetic horizon' defined by the condition p_+ b(x_c^-) = 0, where b(x^-) is the classical potential associated with the field.
Electrons with initial momentum p_+ < b_∞ cannot escape the field and are accelerated to the speed of light, while all positrons can traverse the field.
The classical self-force, calculated using the Landau-Lifshitz equation, shifts the location of the horizon to earlier times x^- < b^-1(p_+).
The quantum wavefunctions exhibit divergences at the classical horizon for electrons, and discontinuities at the past horizon for positrons.
The discontinuities in the positron wavefunctions are interpreted as signaling pair production via the Schwinger effect.

The wavefunctions are noted to be 'almost semiclassical-exact', with the exponent given by the classical Hamilton-Jacobi action and the square root prefactor representing the next-to-leading order WKB term.
The authors use the 'perturbiner' method to construct 'amplitudes' that can be used to calculate observables related to pair creation and radiation, despite the lack of a well-defined S-matrix.

The electromagnetic system studied is proposed as a toy model for exploring analogous questions in the more complex gravitational context, such as the treatment of horizons and strong curvature effects.
The radiated power from the accelerated particles exhibits a divergence at the classical horizon for electrons that cannot escape the field.
There is an 'electromagnetic memory effect' where the final momentum of particles that traverse the field is different from their initial momentum.
The system exhibits a causal structure similar to that of plane wave backgrounds in both electrodynamics and gravity, but with important differences in the existence of a well-defined S-matrix.
The authors note that in this system, the pair production mechanism realizes concretely many properties attributed to Hawking radiation in the gravitational context.
The lack of a Cauchy surface and the violation of unitarity when crossing the horizon are key challenges addressed in the analysis of this electromagnetic system.
The authors emphasize the potential of modern QFT methods, such as the amplitudes approach, to simplify the calculation of observables in classical gravitational wave systems.
